# Closures of the University of Wisconsin Branch Campuses

The University of Wisconsin (UW) System has undergone a significant restructuring of its network of two-year branch campuses, leading to a wave of closures, consolidations, and relocations that began in earnest around 2022. This process represents a multi-stage transformation driven by a confluence of long-term demographic shifts, sustained declines in student enrollment, systemic fiscal pressures within the state, and a major administrative reorganization in 2018 , . The closures are not isolated incidents but part of a deliberate strategy by the UW System to adapt its infrastructure to meet contemporary educational and economic demands, though this strategy has been met with considerable controversy and local impact , . The issue is deeply embedded in Wisconsin's political landscape, with partisan debates centering on the role of state funding, the effectiveness of the 2018 merger, and the future of accessible higher education in rural communities , . Each closure has profound consequences for students seeking associate degrees, for the host counties that own the properties, and for the regional economies that rely on these institutions as workforce hubs , . As of late 2025, eight branch campuses have been officially designated for closure or significant downsizing, while five remain operational, albeit facing their own enrollment challenges , . The vacated campuses present both a financial burden and a potential opportunity for redevelopment, with some counties successfully repurposing the facilities into multi-use community assets , .

## Chronology of Campus Closures and Status Changes

The recent history of the University of Wisconsin's branch campuses is defined by a clear and accelerating timeline of institutional change, moving from initial consolidation to widespread closures. This progression can be broken down into distinct phases, beginning with the landmark 2018 merger of all 13 two-year campuses into branches under seven comprehensive universities , . While intended to improve efficiency, this merger failed to halt a systemic enrollment decline, which subsequently triggered a new wave of closures starting in 2022 , . The process involves various outcomes, including permanent cessation of in-person instruction, transition to exclusively online learning, and strategic relocation to partner institutions , . A detailed examination of each affected campus reveals the scale and pace of this transformation.

The initial phase of closures began in 2022 and 2023, marking the first definitive action to shutter campuses within this restructured system. The first of these was the UW–Platteville Richland campus, announced for closure in November 2022 and officially ceasing in-person classes after the Spring 2023 semester, with an effective closure date of July 1, 2023 , , . It is consistently identified as the first campus to close in this wave of events , . Following this, a second round of closures was announced in October 2023, affecting three additional campuses. These included the UW–Milwaukee Washington County (West Bend) and the UW–Oshkosh at Fond du Lac, both of which officially ceased operations after the Spring 2024 semester, with closures effective June 2024 , . In January 2024, it was announced that the UW–Green Bay at Marinette campus would suspend its in-person classes after the Spring 2024 semester, a move effective June 2024; however, it continues to offer limited online courses and hosts community arts events under its existing lease , .

The third and fourth waves of closures accelerated through 2024 and 2025, demonstrating the increasing urgency of the situation. In March 2024, the UW–Milwaukee Waukesha branch was announced for closure and was subsequently shuttered at the end of the 2023–24 academic year . In June 2024, two more campuses were targeted: the UW–Oshkosh Fox Cities campus was scheduled to close after the Spring 2025 semester (June 2025), and the UW–Stevens Point at Wausau campus announced plans to relocate rather than close entirely , . This relocation to Northcentral Technical College's campus in Wausau for Fall 2026 is a co-location partnership designed to strengthen regional economic alignment and streamline transfer pathways, distinguishing it from a formal closure , . The most recent development detailed in the provided sources is the announcement made on December 13, 2025, concerning the UW–Platteville Baraboo Sauk County campus. This campus was slated to permanently cease all in-person operations on May 22, 2026, following an announcement made on that same day , , . This closure makes it the eighth branch campus to be designated for shutdown or drastic downsizing since 2023 , .

The table below provides a summary of the status and key dates for each affected campus, offering a clear overview of the timeline of these significant institutional changes.

| Affected Campus | Announced Closure Date | Effective Closure / Change Date | Type of Change | Key Details |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **UW–Platteville Richland** | November 2022 | July 1, 2023 | Permanent Closure | First campus closed in the recent wave; ceased in-person instruction after Spring 2023. , , |
| **UW–Milwaukee Washington County** | October 2023 | June 2024 | Permanent Closure | Closed after the Spring 2024 semester. , , |
| **UW–Oshkosh at Fond du Lac** | October 2023 | June 2024 | Permanent Closure | Closed after the Spring 2024 semester. , , |
| **UW–Green Bay at Marinette** | January 2024 | June 2024 | End of In-Person Instruction | Suspended in-person classes; continues limited online courses and community events. , , |
| **UW–Milwaukee Waukesha** | March 2024 | End of 2023–24 Academic Year | Permanent Closure | Shuttered at the end of the 2023–24 academic year. , |
| **UW–Oshkosh Fox Cities** | June 2024 | June 2025 | Permanent Closure | Scheduled to close after the Spring 2025 semester. , , |
| **UW–Stevens Point at Wausau** | June 2024 | Fall 2026 | Relocation | Not a closure; relocating to Northcentral Technical College's campus. , |
| **UW–Platteville Baraboo Sauk County** | December 13, 2025 | May 22, 2026 | Permanent Closure | Permanently ceasing operations; spring 2026 semester will proceed as planned. , , |

This chronological progression underscores a pattern of rapid institutional contraction within the UW System's two-year college sector. The initial closures in 2023 set a precedent, followed by an acceleration of decisions throughout 2024 and 2025. The announcement of the Baraboo Sauk County closure in December 2025 indicates that the pressures driving these decisions have not abated but have instead continued to intensify, necessitating further action even as the biennium concludes , . The variety of responses—from full closure to relocation—also reflects an evolving strategy by the UW System to manage its physical footprint and resources in a challenging environment.

## Root Causes: Enrollment Decline and Financial Pressures

The closures of University of Wisconsin branch campuses are primarily justified by the UW System as a necessary response to severe and sustained declines in student enrollment, a trend that has rendered many campuses financially unsustainable , . This enrollment crisis is the direct result of a complex interplay between shifting demographics, increased competition from other educational institutions, and a challenging fiscal environment exacerbated by state-level policy decisions , . The system-wide attrition highlights a stark divergence between the growth of comprehensive universities and the precipitous decline of the two-year branch campuses .

The most frequently cited driver of the closures is the dramatic drop in student headcount. System-wide, total enrollment across the 13 branch campuses fell by a staggering 22 percent, or 1,092 students, in the fall of 2024 compared to the previous year . This figure stands in sharp contrast to the overall system-wide enrollment increase of 1.2 percent during the same period, illustrating the disproportionate impact on the branch campus model . The individual campus stories paint an even grimmer picture. At UW–Platteville Richland, enrollment plummeted by 83% over a five-year period from 2020 to 2025, falling from over 500 students historically to near-zero in its final semester . Another analysis showed an 84% drop from 567 students in 2014 to just 60 in 2022 following the 2018 merger . Similarly, UW–Stevens Point at Marshfield experienced a nearly 45% decline in enrollment between fall 2023 and fall 2024, reflecting intense systemic pressure . The campus at Wausau saw its numbers drop by 73% between 2015 and 2024, from 978 to 265 students . Projections for the UW–Oshkosh Fox Cities campus were equally dire, predicting it would enroll fewer than 100 students by 2032 . Even the UW–Platteville Baraboo Sauk County campus, which was slated for closure in 2026, saw its fall 2024 enrollment fall to 116-126 students, down from a capacity of 350 and nearly 500 students in 2018 when UW–Platteville assumed oversight , , , . This consistent, system-wide collapse in demand for in-person two-year programs is the central justification for the closures.

This enrollment crisis occurred within a challenging fiscal context for the entire UW System. The institution relies heavily on tuition and fees, which accounted for 58% of its $13.7 billion biennial budget for 2023–25 . Consequently, a reduction in student numbers directly translates to a significant loss of revenue, creating untenable financial situations at campuses that cannot sustain themselves without adequate student populations. The problem was compounded by decades of state funding cuts and tuition freezes. Beginning in 2013, a series of legislative actions froze tuition and cut $66 million from the UW System budget, a move described by experts as effectively defunding the two-year campuses . This was followed by a 14-year freeze on in-state tuition since 2015, which severely constrained the system's ability to generate revenue to offset declining enrollment . The overall ranking of the UW System for public funding declined to 44th out of 50 states in 2024, indicating a persistent challenge in securing adequate state support relative to peers .

Furthermore, the 2017-2018 administrative merger of the 13 two-year colleges into branches of four-year universities, while intended to improve efficiency, may have inadvertently accelerated the enrollment decline at some locations , . Former UW System President Ray Cross advocated for this merger to expand programming and reduce administrative costs, but sources indicate that collaboration between the newly merged units "didn’t come to fruition" system-wide , . At campuses like Richland, the integration led to the loss of dedicated recruitment staff, such as a campus recruiter and an international student program coordinator, which crippled local outreach capabilities post-merger . This suggests that the structural change, rather than solving the enrollment problem, created new challenges that contributed to the downward spiral. The combination of external demographic pressures and internal administrative failures within the post-merger structure created a perfect storm, making the continuation of all branch campuses financially impossible and leading directly to the wave of closures seen in the 2022-2026 period.

## Political and Legislative Context

The closures of the University of Wisconsin branch campuses are deeply entangled in the state's political discourse, serving as a flashpoint in the ongoing debate over public funding for higher education. The issue is framed differently by legislators from opposing parties, with Republicans largely attributing the closures to unavoidable demographic realities and fiscally responsible budgetary decisions, while Democrats point to years of systemic underfunding and a failure of Republican-led legislatures to adequately invest in public institutions , , . This partisan divide shapes public perception and influences the legislative recommendations being considered to address the crisis.

From a Republican perspective, the closures are presented as a logical consequence of demographic trends and a necessary step to ensure fiscal responsibility. During legislative hearings, Republican lawmakers questioned the need for additional state funding, citing declining birth rates as a primary cause for potential future enrollment drops . They argue that the closures reflect market realities and that the focus should be on managing taxpayer dollars efficiently. Republican-controlled state Legislatures are also noted as having imposed fiscal restraints that contributed to the financial decisions made by the UW System . Assembly Speaker Robin Vos famously dismissed Governor Tony Evers’ proposed $856 million increase for the UW System as a "non-starter," highlighting the deep-seated disagreement over funding levels . This viewpoint frames the closures as an unfortunate but inevitable outcome of broader societal shifts, for which the state is not solely responsible.

In stark contrast, Democratic legislators and advocates attribute the closures directly to a prolonged period of underinvestment in public higher education. State Senator Kelda Roys (D-Madison) explicitly linked the closures to "15 years of underfunding public higher education" and warned that the decisions "shut doors of opportunity for young people" in service of "tax breaks for billionaires" , . Similarly, State Senator Sarah Keyeski (D-Lodi) called the closure of the UW–Platteville Baraboo Sauk County campus part of a "trend of two-year colleges closing across our state" and blamed it on a "continuous lack of investment in higher education and in our rural communities" by her Republican colleagues . This narrative positions the closures not as a neutral response to demographics, but as the direct result of policy choices made by the Republican-led legislature, arguing that adequate state funding could have prevented or mitigated the crisis. This perspective emphasizes the social cost of the closures, framing them as a betrayal of access to affordable education for Wisconsin residents.

The political tension extends beyond ideological arguments into concrete legislative actions and vetoes. In one notable instance, a proposal to merge the UW–Milwaukee at Washington County campus with Moraine Park Technical College was put forward and funded in the state budget. However, Governor Tony Evers vetoed the measure, stating that it improperly bypassed the authority of the UW System Board of Regents and reflected a broader legislative failure to provide adequate funding for branch campuses . His veto message underscored his objection to singling out one campus while others faced similar challenges due to inadequate funding, and he asserted that such matters are the purview of the university system's governing board . This event illustrates the power struggle between the executive and legislative branches over the management of state educational institutions. The creation of a bicameral study committee by the Wisconsin Legislature in 2024 to evaluate UW System infrastructure and deliver recommendations further demonstrates the high level of political scrutiny the issue receives . Ultimately, the closures are not merely an administrative decision but a politically charged symbol of the fundamental disagreements over the role, funding, and future of public higher education in Wisconsin.

## Community Impact and Redevelopment

The closure of University of Wisconsin branch campuses creates multifaceted consequences for the host communities, extending far beyond the immediate loss of educational services. A critical distinction is that these campuses are typically owned by the host counties, not the state, which places a direct and often substantial financial burden on local governments . This reality forces counties to grapple with the costs of maintaining abandoned buildings, navigating environmental remediation, and planning for the future use of valuable real estate. At the same time, these vacated properties represent a significant opportunity for redevelopment, with some counties successfully transforming them into vibrant community assets that serve new economic and social functions .

The financial liabilities placed upon host counties are a primary concern. After the UW–Platteville Richland campus closed, Richland County officials described the site as being in disrepair, with coffee cups, pens, and plates left behind, and estimated that bringing the buildings to a minimum usable condition would cost $30 million . The county now faces ongoing monthly utility bills of $10,000–$12,000 for the vacant structures, with no fiscally responsible path identified to preserve them . Similarly, Sauk County, home to the soon-to-be-closed UW–Platteville Baraboo Sauk County campus, assumed $390,000 in operational responsibilities for the property in 2025, including tasks like snow-shoveling and lawn-mowing , . This shift of responsibility from the state-supported university to the local taxpayer creates a significant long-term drain on county budgets, forcing difficult choices between investing in the former campus or other essential services.

However, the story of community impact is not solely one of financial strain. The redevelopment of these campuses offers a pathway to mitigate losses and create new value. The Fond du Lac County redevelopment of the former UW–Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus serves as a powerful case study in proactive and successful repurposing . Using a combination of federal funding, a state grant, and existing revenues, the county transformed the property into a multi-use facility. This includes a 400-seat event center, a 340-seat Prairie Theater for cultural performances, space for law enforcement training, county offices, and a full basketball gym . The project is projected to generate $600,000–$700,000 in annual revenue once fully operational and is expected to create new economic opportunities and cultural attractions for the region, directly addressing local concerns about a lack of engagement for younger residents . This approach demonstrates how a community can turn a liability into an asset.

Other counties have pursued different strategies. Marinette County, where the UW–Green Bay Marinette campus ended its in-person operations, sold 18.6 acres of the campus fieldhouse to the Greater Marinette-Menominee YMCA for $1 . The county allocated $500,000 of its $2 million state grant for closed UW campuses toward improvements for the new owner, showcasing a collaborative approach to redevelopment . Marathon County, which owns the UW–Stevens Point at Wausau campus, is beginning to plan its future use by early 2026, recognizing the importance of finding a productive next chapter for the facility . The overarching challenge for all host communities is to balance the immense cost of maintaining these large properties with the need to find sustainable, economically viable uses that honor the legacy of the campuses while meeting the evolving needs of the region. The varying approaches highlight the diverse ways in which communities are responding to the profound and lasting impact of these closures.

## The Broader Higher Education Landscape

The closures of the University of Wisconsin's branch campuses are not an isolated phenomenon but part of a larger national conversation about the future of two-year colleges in the United States. These institutions have historically served as a crucial gateway to higher education, particularly for students from underserved and rural communities, offering accessible and affordable pathways to associate degrees and transfer to four-year universities . The challenges facing the UW System mirror a broader trend of declining enrollment and financial instability affecting many community colleges across the country, which are grappling with shifting demographics, increased competition, and a changing job market . The UW System's response—consolidation and closure—represents one of several possible strategies being debated nationwide.

One of the core issues is the intense competition from other educational providers, particularly technical colleges and universities. The proliferation of online degree programs has further complicated the landscape, allowing four-year universities to compete directly for students who might have previously enrolled in a traditional two-year college. This dynamic has contributed to the decline in two-year enrollment nationally, which fell by over 17% in the same period that the UW system was experiencing its own struggles . The UW System's own 2018 merger, which integrated two-year campuses into comprehensive universities, was partly motivated by a desire to expand programming and better compete for students . However, as some evidence suggests, this strategy did not universally succeed in reversing enrollment declines and may have created new administrative hurdles . The question of how best to structure the relationship between liberal arts-focused universities and career-and-technical education remains a contentious issue within the state, with former UW System President Ray Cross advocating for a unified system but deeming legislative action unlikely without strong political will .

The financial models of these institutions are also under strain. The heavy reliance on tuition revenue makes them vulnerable to enrollment fluctuations, a fact that became starkly apparent in the UW System . Furthermore, the high cost of maintaining physical campuses, especially in areas with low population density, presents a significant barrier to sustainability. This has led to discussions about transitioning more programs to online delivery, a strategy being implemented at campuses like Marinette . This shift reflects a broader national trend towards hybrid and online learning, but it also raises questions about equity and access for students who may require in-person support services, hands-on training, or reliable internet access that is not always available in rural areas.

Looking ahead, the future of the two-year college model in Wisconsin appears uncertain. While five branch campuses remain open, they all face declining enrollment trends, suggesting the pressures are systemic and ongoing . The state's ranking for public funding for higher education at 44th nationally underscores the chronic under-resourcing that contributes to these challenges . In response to the destabilizing effects of the closures and consolidations, the 2025–27 Biennial Budget includes over $250 million for the UW System, with a portion specifically allocated to help stabilize the system and support campuses statewide . This funding aims to address immediate fallout from the closures, such as layoffs and program cuts, and to ensure that the remaining UW institutions continue to function as vital economic and workforce hubs across the state . However, whether this injection of funds is sufficient to reverse the long-term demographic and financial headwinds remains a critical unanswered question.

## Current Status and Future Outlook

As of late 2025, the University of Wisconsin System has significantly reduced its network of two-year branch campuses, with eight locations either permanently closed, downsized to online-only instruction, or relocated to partner institutions since 2023 , . Five campuses remain fully operational as of the latest available information, continuing to serve students in their respective regions , . However, the long-term stability of this remaining cohort is uncertain, as several of these campuses are also contending with declining enrollment, indicating that the systemic pressures that drove the recent wave of closures are not yet resolved . The future of the two-year college model within the UW System will likely depend on its ability to adapt to demographic shifts, secure stable state funding, and redefine its role in the evolving higher education landscape.

The five campuses that remain open are located in Barron, Manitowoc, Sheboygan, Marshfield, and Rock Counties , . Of these, only UW-Eau Claire Barron County and UW-Whitewater Rock County are projected to see slight enrollment increases in the coming years, according to budget documents released in June 2024 . In contrast, the remaining three—UW-Green Bay Manitowoc, UW-Green Bay Sheboygan, and UW-Stevens Point Marshfield—are all projected to experience steady or modest declines in full-time equivalent (FTE) student numbers . UW-Stevens Point at Marshfield, in particular, has already demonstrated a dramatic enrollment drop of nearly 45% between fall 2023 and fall 2024, making it one of the most vulnerable of the remaining campuses . This data suggests that while the most acute crisis may have passed with the closures of the least viable campuses, the underlying financial and demographic challenges persist and threaten the viability of even the surviving branch campuses.

The fate of the closed campuses is varied, reflecting the differing capacities and priorities of the host counties. Some counties have struggled with the immense financial burden of maintaining abandoned properties. Richland County, for example, faces millions in potential renovation costs and thousands of dollars per month in utilities for the former UW–Platteville Richland site, with no clear path forward for preservation . In other cases, proactive redevelopment has turned liabilities into assets. Fond du Lac County’s successful transformation of the former UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus into a profitable multi-use facility generating revenue is a prime example of a positive outcome . Other counties, like Marinette, have opted for a sale-and-repurpose strategy, transferring ownership of parts of the campus to organizations like the YMCA . The future of these properties will continue to be a focal point for local governance, with the state providing a pool of up to $20 million in redevelopment grants to assist counties in finding new uses for the land and buildings .

In conclusion, the closures of the University of Wisconsin branch campuses represent a pivotal moment in the state's public higher education system. Driven by a perfect storm of demographic decline, systemic underfunding, and the unintended consequences of a major administrative merger, the process has reshaped the landscape of accessible education in Wisconsin. While the immediate crisis has led to the consolidation of the system's physical footprint, the long-term challenges of securing funding, ensuring equitable access, and adapting to a changing world remain unresolved. The actions taken by the remaining campuses and their host counties in the coming years will be crucial in determining the ultimate trajectory of the two-year college model in the state.

However, Governor Tony Evers vetoed the measure, stating that it improperly bypassed the authority of the UW System Board of Regents and reflected a broader legislative failure to provide adequate funding for branch campuses.

His veto message underscored his objection to singling out one campus while others faced similar challenges due to inadequate funding, and he asserted that such matters are the purview of the university system's governing board.
This event illustrates the power struggle between the executive and legislative branches over the management of state educational institutions.

The creation of a bicameral study committee by the Wisconsin Legislature in 2024 to evaluate UW System infrastructure and deliver recommendations further demonstrates the high level of political scrutiny the issue receives.

Ultimately, the closures are not merely an administrative decision but a politically charged symbol of the fundamental disagreements over the role, funding, and future of public higher education in Wisconsin.
The closure of University of Wisconsin branch campuses creates multifaceted consequences for the host communities, extending far beyond the immediate loss of educational services.
A critical distinction is that these campuses are typically owned by the host counties, not the state, which places a direct and often substantial financial burden on local governments.
This reality forces counties to grapple with the costs of maintaining abandoned buildings, navigating environmental remediation, and planning for the future use of valuable real estate.

At the same time, these vacated properties represent a significant opportunity for redevelopment, with some counties successfully transforming them into vibrant community assets that serve new economic and social functions.
The financial liabilities placed upon host counties are a primary concern.

After the UW–Platteville Richland campus closed, Richland County officials described the site as being in disrepair, with coffee cups, pens, and plates left behind, and estimated that bringing the buildings to a minimum usable condition would cost $30 million.
Richland County now faces ongoing monthly utility bills of $10,000–$12,000 for the vacant structures, with no fiscally responsible path identified to preserve them.

Similarly, Sauk County, home to the soon-to-be-closed UW–Platteville Baraboo Sauk County campus, assumed $390,000 in operational responsibilities for the property in 2025, including tasks like snow-shoveling and lawn-mowing.

This shift of responsibility from the state-supported university to the local taxpayer creates a significant long-term drain on county budgets, forcing difficult choices between investing in the former campus or other essential services.
However, the story of community impact is not solely one of financial strain.
The redevelopment of these campuses offers a pathway to mitigate losses and create new value.
The Fond du Lac County redevelopment of the former UW–Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus serves as a powerful case study in proactive and successful repurposing.
Using a combination of federal funding, a state grant, and existing revenues, Fond du Lac County transformed the property into a multi-use facility.
This includes a 400-seat event center, a 340-seat Prairie Theater for cultural performances, space for law enforcement training, county offices, and a full basketball gym.

The project is projected to generate $600,000–$700,000 in annual revenue once fully operational and is expected to create new economic opportunities and cultural attractions for the region, directly addressing local concerns about a lack of engagement for younger residents.
This approach demonstrates how a community can turn a liability into an asset.
Marinette County, where the UW–Green Bay Marinette campus ended its in-person operations, sold 18.6 acres of the campus fieldhouse to the Greater Marinette-Menominee YMCA for $1.
Marinette County allocated $500,000 of its $2 million state grant for closed UW campuses toward improvements for the new owner, showcasing a collaborative approach to redevelopment.
Marathon County, which owns the UW–Stevens Point at Wausau campus, is beginning to plan its future use by early 2026, recognizing the importance of finding a productive next chapter for the facility.

The overarching challenge for all host communities is to balance the immense cost of maintaining these large properties with the need to find sustainable, economically viable uses that honor the legacy of the campuses while meeting the evolving needs of the region.
The varying approaches highlight the diverse ways in which communities are responding to the profound and lasting impact of these closures.
The closures of the University of Wisconsin's branch campuses are not an isolated phenomenon but part of a larger national conversation about the future of two-year colleges in the United States.

These institutions have historically served as a crucial gateway to higher education, particularly for students from underserved and rural communities, offering accessible and affordable pathways to associate degrees and transfer to four-year universities.

The challenges facing the UW System mirror a broader trend of declining enrollment and financial instability affecting many community colleges across the country, which are grappling with shifting demographics, increased competition, and a changing job market.
The UW System's response—consolidation and closure—represents one of several possible strategies being debated nationwide.
One of the core issues is the intense competition from other educational providers, particularly technical colleges and universities.

The proliferation of online degree programs has further complicated the landscape, allowing four-year universities to compete directly for students who might have previously enrolled in a traditional two-year college.
This dynamic has contributed to the decline in two-year enrollment nationally, which fell by over 17% in the same period that the UW system was experiencing its own struggles.
The UW System's own 2018 merger, which integrated two-year campuses into comprehensive universities, was partly motivated by a desire to expand programming and better compete for students.
However, as some evidence suggests, this strategy did not universally succeed in reversing enrollment declines and may have created new administrative hurdles.

The question of how best to structure the relationship between liberal arts-focused universities and career-and-technical education remains a contentious issue within the state, with former UW System President Ray Cross advocating for a unified system but deeming legislative action unlikely without strong political will.
The financial models of these institutions are also under strain.
The heavy reliance on tuition revenue makes them vulnerable to enrollment fluctuations, a fact that became starkly apparent in the UW System.
Furthermore, the high cost of maintaining physical campuses, especially in areas with low population density, presents a significant barrier to sustainability.
This has led to discussions about transitioning more programs to online delivery, a strategy being implemented at campuses like Marinette.

This shift reflects a broader national trend towards hybrid and online learning, but it also raises questions about equity and access for students who may require in-person support services, hands-on training, or reliable internet access that is not always available in rural areas.
Looking ahead, the future of the two-year college model in Wisconsin appears uncertain.
While five branch campuses remain open, they all face declining enrollment trends, suggesting the pressures are systemic and ongoing.
The state's ranking for public funding for higher education at 44th nationally underscores the chronic under-resourcing that contributes to these challenges.

In response to the destabilizing effects of the closures and consolidations, the 2025–27 Biennial Budget includes over $250 million for the UW System, with a portion specifically allocated to help stabilize the system and support campuses statewide.

This funding aims to address immediate fallout from the closures, such as layoffs and program cuts, and to ensure that the remaining UW institutions continue to function as vital economic and workforce hubs across the state.

As of late 2025, the University of Wisconsin System has significantly reduced its network of two-year branch campuses, with eight locations either permanently closed, downsized to online-only instruction, or relocated to partner institutions since 2023.
Five campuses remain fully operational as of the latest available information, continuing to serve students in their respective regions.

However, the long-term stability of this remaining cohort is uncertain, as several of these campuses are also contending with declining enrollment, indicating that the systemic pressures that drove the recent wave of closures are not yet resolved.

The future of the two-year college model within the UW System will likely depend on its ability to adapt to demographic shifts, secure stable state funding, and redefine its role in the evolving higher education landscape.
The five campuses that remain open are located in Barron, Manitowoc, Sheboygan, Marshfield, and Rock Counties.
Of these, only UW-Eau Claire Barron County and UW-Whitewater Rock County are projected to see slight enrollment increases in the coming years, according to budget documents released in June 2024.

In contrast, the remaining three—UW-Green Bay Manitowoc, UW-Green Bay Sheboygan, and UW-Stevens Point Marshfield—are all projected to experience steady or modest declines in full-time equivalent (FTE) student numbers.

UW-Stevens Point at Marshfield, in particular, has already demonstrated a dramatic enrollment drop of nearly 45% between fall 2023 and fall 2024, making it one of the most vulnerable of the remaining campuses.

This data suggests that while the most acute crisis may have passed with the closures of the least viable campuses, the underlying financial and demographic challenges persist and threaten the viability of even the surviving branch campuses.
The fate of the closed campuses is varied, reflecting the differing capacities and priorities of the host counties.
Some counties have struggled with the immense financial burden of maintaining abandoned properties.

Richland County, for example, faces millions in potential renovation costs and thousands of dollars per month in utilities for the former UW–Platteville Richland site, with no clear path forward for preservation.
In other cases, proactive redevelopment has turned liabilities into assets.
Fond du Lac County’s successful transformation of the former UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus into a profitable multi-use facility generating revenue is a prime example of a positive outcome.
Other counties, like Marinette, have opted for a sale-and-repurpose strategy, transferring ownership of parts of the campus to organizations like the YMCA.

The future of these properties will continue to be a focal point for local governance, with the state providing a pool of up to $20 million in redevelopment grants to assist counties in finding new uses for the land and buildings.
The closures of the University of Wisconsin branch campuses represent a pivotal moment in the state's public higher education system.

Driven by a perfect storm of demographic decline, systemic underfunding, and the unintended consequences of a major administrative merger, the process has reshaped the landscape of accessible education in Wisconsin.

While the immediate crisis has led to the consolidation of the system's physical footprint, the long-term challenges of securing funding, ensuring equitable access, and adapting to a changing world remain unresolved.
The actions taken by the remaining campuses and their host counties in the coming years will be crucial in determining the ultimate trajectory of the two-year college model in the state.

UW-Platteville closing Baraboo campus in 2026, citing low enrollment
====================================================================

 [![Image 1: Portrait of Kelly Meyerhofer](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/02/09/PMJS/72544461007-kelly-meyerhofer-020124.jpg?crop=4127,4128,x0,y51&width=48&height=48&format=pjpg&auto=webp) Kelly Meyerhofer](https://www.jsonline.com/staff/9722381002/kelly-meyerhofer/)

Milwaukee Journal Sentinel

Updated Oct. 17, 2025, 4:09 p.m. CT

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=227386193957280&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jsonline.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2Feducation%2F2025%2F10%2F17%2Fuw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026%2F86750472007%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jsonline.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2Feducation%2F2025%2F10%2F17%2Fuw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026%2F86750472007%2F&text=UW-Platteville%20closing%20Baraboo%20campus%20in%202026%2C%20citing%20low%20enrollment&via=journalsentinel)[](mailto:?subject=UW-Platteville%20closing%20Baraboo%20campus%20in%202026%2C%20citing%20low%20enrollment%20-%20from%20Journal%20Sentinel&body=UW-Platteville%20closing%20Baraboo%20campus%20in%202026%2C%20citing%20low%20enrollment%0A%0AThe%20closure%20of%20UW-Platteville%20Baraboo%20Sauk%20County%20is%20the%20eighth%20of%20the%2013%20UW%20branch%20campuses%20to%20either%20close%20or%20downsize%20since%202023.%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20jsonline.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jsonline.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2Feducation%2F2025%2F10%2F17%2Fuw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026%2F86750472007%2F)

0:00

/

\--

Keep Watching

The University of Wisconsin-Platteville is closing its Baraboo campus at the end of the school year, eliminating an [educational option that has been around since 1968](https://www.uwplatt.edu/baraboo/history).

It's the eighth of the 13 UW branch campuses to either close or downsize since 2023, underscoring the financial pressures and enrollment problems these schools have faced.

UW-Platteville Chancellor Tammy Evetovich, who declined an interview, cited declining enrollment as the main driver of the decision.

Initially designed to accommodate 350 students, UW-Platteville Baraboo Sauk County enrolled 126 this fall. That's down from nearly 500 in 2018, the year UW-Platteville absorbed oversight of the campus.

UW-Platteville agreed to honor the Baraboo campus tuition rate for students who transfer to the main campus next fall. The university is developing plans for each of the 22 faculty and staff who work at the campus.

The campus' operating budget for its final year is $1.8 million. Its last day will be May 22, 2026.

What is a branch campus?
------------------------

The Baraboo campus in Sauk County, often called "Boo-U" by locals, began as an extension of UW-Madison and later joined the UW Colleges. The 13 branch campuses within UW Colleges operated as affordable two-year launch pads for students to pursue associate's degrees close to home before transferring to a four-year university.About a decade ago, the UW Colleges began seeing a steep drop in students because there were fewer Wisconsin high school students for campuses to recruit. The campuses also faced competition from technical colleges.

Madison Area Technical College has campuses in Portage and Reedsburg, both of which are about a half-hour drive away from UW-Baraboo.

In 2018, the branch campuses were placed under the oversight of four-year UW institutions in an attempt to keep them open. Since then, five — [UW-Platteville Richland](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2022/11/22/university-of-wisconsin-platteville-richland-center-to-axe-in-person-classes/69671077007/), [UW-Milwaukee at Washington County](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2023/10/17/uw-washington-county-uw-fond-du-lac-ending-in-person-degree-programs/71208221007/), [UW-Milwaukee at Waukesha](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/03/11/uw-milwaukee-at-waukesha-to-close-after-spring-2025-semester/72929987007/), [UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2023/10/17/uw-washington-county-uw-fond-du-lac-ending-in-person-degree-programs/71208221007/) and [UW-Oshkosh Fox Cities](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/06/13/university-of-wisconsin-oshkosh-closing-uw-fox-cities-campus/74083903007/) have closed. A sixth,  [UW-Green Bay Marinette](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/01/19/uw-green-bay-marinette-ending-in-person-classes-after-spring-2024-semester/72289101007/), has ended in-person classes. A [seventh, UW-Stevens Point Marathon County](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/09/11/uw-stevens-point-wausau-to-relocate-to-northcentral-technical-college/86073681007/), is relocating its campus to the local technical college in fall 2026.

Redevelopment plans underway for UW-Baraboo Sauk County campus
--------------------------------------------------------------

The 63-acre campus is jointly owned and maintained by Sauk County and the City of Baraboo.

"We're pretty optimistic about the future of our campus," then-Baraboo City Administrator Casey Bradley [told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel in 2023.](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2023/01/27/other-counties-are-looking-at-their-local-uw-campus-after-uw-richland/69832459007/)

But concerns grew more recently.

Sauk County in 2025 took on the responsiblity for and covered some operational tasks that UW-Platteville had previously covered, such as snow-shoveling and lawn-mowing. The amount totaled $390,000.

In June, UW-Platteville moved the campus from four buildings into one. The consolidation, coupled with the campus' falling enrollment pattern, pushed county officials to explore redevelopment options.

Sauk County [sought proposals from firms this summer](https://www.co.sauk.wi.us/countyadministration/baraboo-sauk-county-campus-redevelopment-plan-sauk-county-administration) and aims to finalize a redevelopment plan by next June. It plans to pay for the work with a state grant available to counties with closed UW campuses.

"We wanted to be in front of any decision that was made for us," county development director Melanie Platt-Gibson said about the decision to issue a request for proposals months before the campus closure announcement came.

Sauk County learned of the campus' closure around 12:30 p.m. Oct. 17, just minutes before media outlets.

Other UW campuses repurposed into housing, K12 school, community center
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

For 57 years, the Baraboo campus has enriched the community with arts, athletics and culture. Baraboo Mayor Rob Nelson said he personally enjoyed using the library and participating in theater productions.

"Those sort of connections will be sorely missed," he wrote in an email. "While this decision was beyond our control, it does not deter us from working with the community to ensure that the campus remains a vibrant resource for Baraboo and Sauk County residents for years to come."

Rep. Karen DeSanto, D-Baraboo, laid blame on the Republican-controlled Legislature for failing to adequately fund UW campuses for nearly a decade.

Sen. Sarah Keyeski, another Democrat whose district includes the campus, said having two-year campuses gives people more flexibility in their education.

"It’s upsetting to see this trend of two-year colleges closing across our state," she said in a statement.

Universities of Wisconsin President Jay Rothman told state lawmakers earlier this year the remaining branch campuses would stay open if his request for an $855 million budget increase over the next two years was approved. The budget passed this summer included a $256 million increase.

At other shuttered branch campuses, the four-year universities that were in charge of them have largely abandoned their presence post-closure, leaving decisions to county and city officials.

[Hundreds of homes are slated to replace](https://www.jsonline.com/story/communities/west/2025/01/17/heres-whats-next-in-the-redevelopment-process-at-uwm-waukesha-campus/77746199007/) the former Waukesha campus. In Washington County, a [private Christian school is poised to buy the former West Bend campus](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/08/27/washington-county-moves-to-sell-former-uw-campus-to-ozaukee-christian/85701018007/). Fond du Lac County converted the former UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus into an events center and community space. Richland County, so far unable to generate interest from outside buyers, has been slowly dismantling its former campus piece by piece.

_Kelly Meyerhofer has covered higher education in Wisconsin since 2018. Contact her at kmeyerhofer@gannett.com or 414-223-5168. Follow her on X (Twitter) at @KellyMeyerhofer._

The University of Wisconsin-Platteville will close their Baraboo Sauk County campus at the end of the 2025-26 school year due to low enrollment, the university [announced](https://www.wispolitics.com/2025/uw-platteville-announces-it-will-cease-operations-on-baraboo-sauk-county-campus/) Friday.

Only 126 students [enrolled](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/10/17/uw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026/86750472007/) for the fall semester when the campus initially prepared for 350. Just seven years ago, when the branch [merged](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/10/17/uw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026/86750472007/) with UW-Platteville in 2018, nearly 500 students were enrolled.

Baraboo is the eighth branch campus to close since 2022, when the [UW-System ordered](https://www.dailycardinal.com/article/2024/06/1-year-after-richland-how-a-rural-wisconsin-community-reckons-with-losing-their-university) UW-Platteville’s other branch campus in Richland Center to close.

UW-Platteville Chancellor Tammy K. Evetovich [said](https://www.wispolitics.com/2025/uw-platteville-announces-it-will-cease-operations-on-baraboo-sauk-county-campus/) in a statement the decision to close Baraboo wasn’t made lightly, but they need to focus efforts to best serve the region and the students.

“Student success is at the heart of our mission,” Evetovich said in the statement. “We are providing additional support and resources to ensure students can transition smoothly to our main campus to complete their programs or find the path forward that best meets their needs.”

Operations will [end](https://www.wispolitics.com/2025/uw-platteville-announces-it-will-cease-operations-on-baraboo-sauk-county-campus/) on May 22, 2026. UW-Platteville will allow students currently enrolled at the Baraboo campus to transfer to its main campus, and the university [said](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/10/17/uw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026/86750472007/) they will honor the Baraboo tuition rate for those students next fall. UW-Platteville [said](https://www.wispolitics.com/2025/uw-platteville-announces-it-will-cease-operations-on-baraboo-sauk-county-campus/) they are also developing plans for the branch faculty and staff, but specific details have not been released.

**Blame laid on lagging state funding**

Rep. Karen DeSanto, D-Baraboo, [expressed](https://www.wispolitics.com/2025/rep-desanto-statement-on-the-may-2026-closing-of-the-university-of-wisconsin-platteville-baraboo-campus/) her disappointment on the closure in a statement Friday and blamed the Republican-controlled Legislature.

“This is part of a greater trend of closing 2 year campuses that have suffered at the hand of nearly a decade of insufficient funding in the state budget due to Republicans’ lack of investment in the Universities of Wisconsin,” DeSanto said in the statement.

While Gov. Tony Evers initially [proposed](https://www.dailycardinal.com/article/2025/02/evers-proposes-over-856-million-investment-in-uw-system-in-2025-budget-address?fbclid=IwY2xjawNeCFtleHRuA2FlbQIxMQBicmlkETFGQ0tHZ1h6c2RlRFQ3anp5AR6EpbFSS5KO4k-r19k_56YsrcSQyFH0CjD_vVes3OoXtVDZ-mJ8XL0XxH8BwQ_aem_Z9joowKvF4sVxCL7-klmzA) $856 million toward the UW System for the 2025-27 budget, he and Republican lawmakers [agreed](https://www.dailycardinal.com/article/2025/07/evers-lawmakers-agree-to-increase-uw-system-funding-by-256-million) on $256 million instead, the largest state funding increase in 20 years.

The state currently [provides](https://wisconsinwatch.org/2025/10/wisconsin-college-affordability-higher-education-cost-tuition-school-study/) 20% of the UW System’s budget, half of what it provided a few decades ago. A recent study [ranks](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/10/15/wisconsin-ranks-among-the-worst-for-college-affordability-in-new-report/86680705007/) Wisconsin at 46th nationally in higher education affordability.

**UW System’s string of branch closures**

Enjoy what you're reading? Get content from The Daily Cardinal delivered to your inbox

The Baraboo Sauk campus closure will be the [eighth](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/10/17/uw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026/86750472007/) UW System branch to close or downsize since 2023 due to low enrollment. UW-Platteville Richland, UW-Milwaukee at Washington County and UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac [closed](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/10/17/uw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026/86750472007/) in 2024. UW-Milwaukee at Waukesha and UW-Oshkosh Fox Cities [closed](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/10/17/uw-platteville-to-close-its-baraboo-sauk-county-campus-in-2026/86750472007/) this past spring.

UW-Stevens Point Wausau will [relocate](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2025/09/11/uw-stevens-point-wausau-to-relocate-to-northcentral-technical-college/86073681007/) near Northcentral Technical College in fall 2026. This comes as fewer high school graduates [pursue](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/03/11/uw-milwaukee-at-waukesha-to-close-after-spring-2025-semester/72929987007/) college degrees, instead [turning](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/03/11/uw-milwaukee-at-waukesha-to-close-after-spring-2025-semester/72929987007/) toward technical programs that will prepare them for the workforce.

In 2018, the UW System’s four-year universities [took](https://www.wisconsin.edu/news/archive/uw-system-restructuring-is-given-seal-of-approval-by-the-higher-learning-commission/) over the 13 UW Colleges, now known as branch campuses, in order to consolidate efforts amid declining enrollment.

Since, some faculty at branch campus faculty [said](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/03/11/uw-milwaukee-at-waukesha-to-close-after-spring-2025-semester/72929987007/) the merge hasn’t worked as intended because universities haven’t helped enough with restructuring of the campuses, instead prioritizing recruiting for the main campus at the expense of the branches and complicating the transfer process.

After this spring, five branch campuses will remain including UW-Eau Claire Barron County, UW-Green Bay Manitowoc, UW-Green Bay Sheboygan, UW-Stevens Point Marshfield and UW-Whitewater Rock County. All [except](https://www.uwgb.edu/CMSAssets/ISE/dashboard.asp) UW-Green Bay Manitowoc also [face](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2023/10/17/uw-washington-county-uw-fond-du-lac-ending-in-person-degree-programs/71208221007/) declining enrollment, though there haven’t been any reports of their closures in the near future.

The Daily Cardinal has been covering the University and Madison community since 1892. Please consider giving today.

UW-Platteville (UW Platteville)

The Universities of Wisconsin branch campus in West Baraboo will close at the end of the school year, officials announced Friday.

The UW-Platteville Baraboo Sauk County is set to close after a steep decline in enrollment. The two-year campus hit an enrollment peak in 2000 with 758 students. Enrollment on the campus hit an all time low this semester with 116 students.

Baraboo Sauk County is the eighth branch campus to be closed or dramatically downsized since 2023. It is also the second branch campus under the management of UW-Platteville to be shut down after the campus in Richland County was shuttered in July 2023.

“This decision was not made lightly,” UW-Platteville Chancellor Tammy Evetovich said in the announcement Friday. “Enrollment continues to decline on that campus, and we are committed to being good partners with the city and county by ensuring the campus can be used in ways that best serve the region.”

Enrollment on UW’s branch campuses has steadily declined in recent years, however campus faculty and staff, as well as residents of affected communities, have blamed UW administration officials for decades of decision making that deprioritized maintaining the two-year campuses.

State Sen. Kelda Roys (D-Madison) blamed the closures on Republican budget decisions.

“Campus closures and the march towards consolidation is a result of Republican politicians viewing higher education as a luxury good that only those who can afford it deserve,” she said in a statement. “In their view, UW is just another cost preventing them from giving more public money to their billionaire campaign backers. The ‘budget shortfalls’ that led to this closure were manufactured over the last 15 years by right-wing politicians who systematically divested from public higher education while strangling UW’s ability to manage its own financial affairs.”

Citing declining enrollment, UW-Platteville will shutter Baraboo Sauk County campus
===================================================================================

The announcement comes 2 years after UW-Platteville ended in-person classes at its Richland Center campus

By [Anya van Wagtendonk](https://www.wpr.org/person/anya-van-wagtendonk "Posts by Anya van Wagtendonk")

October 17, 2025

![Image 2: A blue sign reading "University of Wisconsin-Platteville" stands on the schools' campus.](https://www.wpr.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/img-6685-scaled.jpg)

A sign on UW-Platteville’s campus. _Miranda Suarez/WPR_

The University of Wisconsin-Platteville will shutter its Baraboo Sauk County campus at the end of this school year, according to an announcement Friday.

In a statement, UW-Platteville Chancellor Tammy Evetovich said the decision follows declining enrollment and was “not made lightly.”

“We remain dedicated to supporting our students, faculty and staff through this transition,” she said. “Student success is at the heart of our mission, and we are providing additional support and resources to ensure students can transition smoothly to our main campus to complete their programs or find the path forward that best meets their needs.”

Operations will cease on May 22, 2026, the statement says.

The announcement comes amid financial concerns for the campus, which offers primarily associate degrees, alongside one type of bachelor’s degree. Last year, the Sauk County Board of Supervisors [voted to spend $390,000 on maintenance](https://www.wpr.org/news/sauk-county-board-funds-uw-branch-campus) for the campus after the university projected that size of a budget deficit.

In her statement, Evetovich alluded to the local investment, saying that the school is “committed to being good partners with the city and county by ensuring the campus can be used in ways that best serve the region.”

The announcement comes almost exactly three years after UW-Platteville [announced](https://www.wpr.org/education/uw-platteville-richland-campus-july-1-close-in-person) the end of in-person instruction at its Richland Center campus. That change took place in 2023, [sparking concern](https://www.wpr.org/economy/uw-system-campus-richland-center-local-officials-college-enrollment) that other two-year campuses across the state could see similar changes.

In recent years, UW-Milwaukee closed its Waukesha campus, and in-person classes have ended at its Washington County campus. UW-Green Bay has likewise ended in-person classes at its Marinette County campus, as has UW-Oshkosh at its Fond du Lac campus.

Dec. 10, 2024, 5:03 a.m. CT

[![Image 1](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/12/06/PMJS/76830568007-mjs-uw-branch-campuses-close-and-repurpose-buildings-5.jpg?crop=4496,2530,x2,y414&width=660&height=372&format=pjpg&auto=webp)](https://www.jsonline.com/picture-gallery/news/education/2024/12/10/uw-branch-campuses-repurpose-buildings/76829971007/)Wisconsin counties with shuttered University of Wisconsin branch campuses are reimagining the properties to serve a range of purposes including senior housing, K-12 classroom space, even a wedding venue.

The transformations of these sites come after years of declining enrollment and financial pressures at the two-year campuses previously known as UW Colleges. A 2018 merger placed these branch campuses under the oversight of various four-year UW institutions. But the hemorrhaging of students continued amid demographic challenges and competition with nearby technical colleges.

Since 2023, five branch campuses have closed or will close by the end of this school year. A sixth campus has ended in-person instruction. Unlike four-year institutions that are considered state property, the branch campuses are owned by the counties where they are located.

A [bill signed into state law earlier this year](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/04/01/communities-losing-uw-branch-campus-may-get-2-million-to-redevelop/73147902007/) offered up to $2 million in grant money to help counties redevelop their campuses. A total of $20 million is available from the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation. No counties have received the money to date, but one is nearing a final contract and four have secured application materials.

Here's what to know about redevelopment plans for your local UW branch campus:

UW-Milwaukee at Waukesha to be demolished
-----------------------------------------

Waukesha County plans to demolish the [campus after it closes in June](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/03/11/uw-milwaukee-at-waukesha-to-close-after-spring-2025-semester/72929987007/) and [transform the site into hundreds of homes.](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/10/25/waukesha-advises-uw-waukesha-campus-turn-into-mixed-housing/75829774007/)

![Image 2: Tashaun McCombs, a sophomore from Menomonee Falls, shoots baskets between classes in the field house gymnasium at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee Waukesha campus in Waukesha on Monday, March 11, 2024. The Waukesha campus will close at the end of the spring 2025 semester, eliminating an educational option that has been around since 1966.](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/12/10/what-wisconsin-counties-are-doing-with-their-closed-uw-branch-campuses/76736263007/)

The city of Waukesha Plan Commission [in late November postponed a vote to change the land use of the site from institutional to residential](https://www.gmtoday.com/the_freeman/news/plan-commission-postpones-uwm-waukesha-campus-amendment-decision/article_0fe44860-6240-51b1-a0c6-30badfd92cab.html?=/&subcategory=241%7CRunning). The delay was procedural and doesn't change the county's timeline to approve the mixed residential development plan in January, Waukesha County Parks and Land Use Director Dale Shaver said.

The redevelopment will place valuable land back on the tax roll, he said. The county has already released marketing materials to attract interested developers and anticipates putting out a request for proposals in February.

Waukesha County anticipates using the grant money on demolition costs, county spokeswoman Hillary Mintz said.

Local school district expresses interest in UW-Oshkosh Fox Cities
-----------------------------------------------------------------

What will come of [UW-Oshkosh Fox Cities after it ends in-person classes next June](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/06/13/university-of-wisconsin-oshkosh-closing-uw-fox-cities-campus/74083903007/) is less clear.

Winnebago County and Outagamie County jointly own the land and [facilities of the Menasha campus](https://www.uwosh.edu/fox/community/cac/event-planning/), including the [Barlow Planetarium](https://www.uwosh.edu/barlow/), [Communication Arts Center](https://www.uwosh.edu/fox/community/cac/), [University Children's Center](https://www.uwosh.edu/fox/community/ucc/), [Weis Earth Science Museum](https://www.uwosh.edu/weis/) and a field house.

![Image 3: Signs point to the many facilities located on the University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh at Fox Cities campus.](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/06/24/PAPN/74197556007-apc-uw-oshkosh-fox-cities-9220-062424-wag.jpg?width=660&height=432&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

The counties are working on a plan for the Menasha School District and an outside partner to use the buildings for educational purposes. Details are still being hammered out, but those involved were optimistic.

" (There's) a whole bunch of inside baseball right now that we’re trying to get lined up," Winnebago County Executive Jon Doemel said, noting the plan would need approval from two county boards, a school board and potentially others as well.

If it falls through, Doemel estimated the cost to maintain the buildings could be as much as $800,000 annually.

A community awareness meeting is scheduled for 7 p.m Dec. 12 at the Barlow Planetarium, 1478 Midway Road, Menasha.

UW-Milwaukee at Washington County also getting interest from school districts
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

The [West Bend campus closed last June](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2023/10/17/uw-washington-county-uw-fond-du-lac-ending-in-person-degree-programs/71208221007/), and Washington County is working on a plan for the campus to continue serving an educational purpose.

![Image 4: Psychology professor Tricia Wessel engages with students exiting the building Tuesday, Sept. 27, 2022, at the University of Wisconsin Milwaukee - Washington County in West Bend, Wis.](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/presto/2022/09/27/PMJS/98c9312b-121e-4362-a324-26a3a8aa5053-MJS_09272022__UWMbranchcampuses__EC255123.jpg?width=660&height=414&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

The West Bend School District has expressed interest in using 10% to 15% of the campus space for its alternative education programming, Washington County Executive Josh Schoemann said. Separately, K-12 superintendents across the county sent a formal letter of interest about using some space for special needs services in partnership with the region's Cooperative Educational Service Agency.

The districts may become "anchor tenants" of the space and cover the operational costs of the facility, which are estimated to be $500,000 and $750,000 annually, he said. Lease and operating agreements are expected be formalized next year.

The county is mulling a senior community center, child care center and some other options for the rest of the campus. Schoemann said partnering with outside organizations, such as the local YMCA or a school district, will be key to maintaining some of what the campus provided the commuity, like theater and recreational opportunities.

"We want to get those things back in there, but that is just not something county government does," he said.

Washington County has not yet applied for the grant money but anticipates doing so when plans firm up, he said.

Fond du Lac County sees UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus as revenue generator
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

At the former [UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2023/10/17/uw-washington-county-uw-fond-du-lac-ending-in-person-degree-programs/71208221007/) campus, wedding bells are replacing school bells.

Fond du Lac County turned the campus building into the [Prairie Theater and Events Center](https://www.fdlco.wi.gov/departments/departments-a-f/fond-du-lac-county-campus/performing-arts-event-center), said Josh Boyenga, an assistant to Fond du Lac County Executive Sam Kaufman. Classrooms and the commons space overlooking a prairie landscape are available to rent for trainings, conferences and events, including weddings. Over Halloween, for example, there was a performance of "Rocky Horror Picture Show."

![Image 5: The Prairie Theater on the former UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus on is available to be rented out for theater groups and business meetings. The 345 seat theater recently featured the production of 'All Is Calm, The Christmas Truce of 1914'.](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/12/06/PMJS/76829860007-mjs-uw-branch-campuses-close-and-repurpose-buildings-3.jpg?width=660&height=440&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Reservations are coming in to rent the gymnasium for volleyball tournaments, he said. There's also talk of a pickleball league forming.

The county is turning the art building into a law enforcement training center, Boyenga said. Renovations are underway to build a "mock jail." The pond on the property is deep enough to do dive trainings for officers. This could create a revenue stream from out-of-county police departments.

Over the next few months, the county is moving its human services department to the campus, he said. That will pair well with the county's plan to sell the land surrounding the campus buildings and turn it into senior housing.

"We’re pretty far in the process of redeveloping it," Boyenga said of the campus' transformation. "It was all about what can we do to make this not a taxpayer burden?"

![Image 6: Once the hub of the cafeteria on the grounds of the former UW-Oshkosh Fond du Lac campus, it is now part of the Prairie Theater and Event Center where the theater and classrooms are available to be rented out.](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/12/06/PMJS/76829864007-mjs-uw-branch-campuses-close-and-repurpose-buildings-7.jpg?width=660&height=389&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Richland County faces tough decisions on UW-Platteville Richland campus
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Richland County was the [first to see its campus close](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2022/11/22/university-of-wisconsin-platteville-richland-center-to-axe-in-person-classes/69671077007/) and it is furthest behind in redevelopment.

"We're grappling with significant decisions," Richland County administrator Candace Pesch said. "We're a rural community. We don’t have the economic development opportunities that these larger cities do. Nobody’s come forward to say 'we’d love to take this off your hands.'"

![Image 7: Road Rallye participants make their way to their cars to line up Friday, April 28, 2023, before the University of Wisconsin-Platteville Richland Campus closes its doors. The spring tradition is a scavenger hunt with teams of students and faculty driving around the city searching for answers to questions that leads to a secret location where everyone meets up for a party in Richland Center, Wis.](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/12/10/what-wisconsin-counties-are-doing-with-their-closed-uw-branch-campuses/76736263007/)

A viability study put a $20 million price tag on renovating all campus buildings, she said. Building new would cost even more. The theater and student center, for example, need significant repairs, but the community theater group doesn't have funding to sustain a project of that scale.

"Is there anyone that’s going to want to come in and put $4 million into a 60-year old building?" Pesch asked. "That’s what (the county board is) wrestling with. Is there an opportunity for future use?"

A county committee is considering whether to shutter buildings, which essentially means slotting them for demolition.

"This has been such an emotional time," Pesch said. "It's such a trememdous loss for the community, and it’s been very difficult for them to come to terms with where we’re at. The board is doing the best they can to make data-driven decisions and spend taxpayer money in the most responsible way they can."

UW-Green Bay takes different approach with Marinette campus
-----------------------------------------------------------

[UW-Green Bay Marinette](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/01/19/uw-green-bay-marinette-ending-in-person-classes-after-spring-2024-semester/72289101007/) ended in-person classes last June but continues to have a presence on the campus, running the theater, maintaining the buildings and offering a handful of online classes.

"UW-Green Bay remains under the obligations of the current lease and will do so in a fashion that meets its operational strategy at the campus," university spokesperson Kristin Bouchard said.

![Image 8: The UW-Green Bay Marinette campus in northern Wisconsin is surrounded by forests.](https://www.jsonline.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/01/20/PMJS/72289621007-marinette-outdoors-10.jpg?width=660&height=440&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Marinette County administrator John Lefebvre said the one exception is the fieldhouse, which the county took control of about a year and a half ago. The county provides the space to a community pool association rent free on the condition the nonprofit covers the operational costs.

Bouchard said UW-Green Bay has no plans to end its current operation of the campus and will continue to maintain campus buildings. The university is open to assessing ideas for alternative uses for the space if an opportunity arose and the county supported it.

Seven UW branch campuses left, with some showing enrollment growth
------------------------------------------------------------------

Seven branch campuses remain open with no closure plans announced: UW-Baraboo/Sauk County, UW-Whitewater Rock County, UW-Green Bay Sheboygan, UW-Green Bay Manitowoc, UW-Eau Claire Barron County, UW-Stevens Point Marshfield and UW-Stevens Point Wausau.

Enrollment at three of these campuses — Baraboo/Sauk County, Marshfield and Wausau — [fell this fall from the previous year, while the others saw increases](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/09/23/uw-system-releases-branch-campus-enrollment-estimates-following-outcry/75345927007/). UW System President Jay Rothman has pledged to keep them open if the state approves his [request for an $855 million budget increase over the next two years.](https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2024/08/19/uw-asks-for-massive-state-increase-to-fund-tuition-freeze-worker-raises/74783677007/)

_Kelly Meyerhofer covers higher education in Wisconsin. Contact her at_ [_kmeyerhofer@gannett.com_](mailto:kmeyerhofer@gannett.com) _or 414-223-5168. Follow her on X (Twitter) at_ [_@KellyMeyerhofer_](https://twitter.com/KellyMeyerhofer)_._

FOND DU LAC, Wis. (WLUK) -- Five Universities of Wisconsin two-year colleges [have closed](https://fox11online.com/news/crisis-in-the-classroom/university-wisconsin-oshkosh-fox-cities-campus-closing-two-year-community-junior-college-universities-system) in the past three years. In Fond du Lac, they're moving quickly to redevelop one of those schools.

WLUK

UW-Oshkosh at Fond du Lac is one of the various two-year UW campuses that has closed in recent years. And though it's been just over a year, the county has already re-opened the space for events and found other ways for it to become financially sustainable on its own. So let's have a look inside.

"It was really just a matter of walking through this building a few times and coming up with ideas," said Fond du Lac County Executive Sam Kaufman.

Starting with the primary way to generate revenue.

"And this room is actually set up for events," said Kaufman, referring to the Winnebago room in the main lobby. "We can actually hold up to 400 people now."

The adjacent Prairie Theater is the only venue like it in Fond du Lac, holding 340 seats. The Prairie Theater hosts plays, musicals and comedy shows.

"There's not a younger generation that is really moving into our community, and when we start talking to them it's just that there's nothing to do," said Kaufman. "And I think that was the misconception about the area, because there are things to do here. But now we start coming in and thinking, ok let's turn this into an event center."

Kaufman says he expects the campus will generate $600,000-700,000 per year when fully open. The current revenue already exceeds the expenses.

The county used federal funding, a state grant and existing revenues to redevelop the space.

It's also close to a deal to sell 12 acres for senior housing.

Other uses include training for law enforcement, correctional officers, county employees consolidated from outside buildings, a state senator office and a full basketball gym with batting cages on the side.

"Basically to create an area that benefits the citizens of our county with services," said Kaufman on the goal of the campus, "but also to provide an atmosphere for the younger generation to know there's events going on, really at no cost to our taxpayers. That's really what we were trying to accomplish."

Kaufman expects even with all the renovations, no county tax dollars will be used.
